_comment: Exported symbol names -> the component they belong to.
Read by identify-elf-presence.py alongside elf-soname-map.json and
elf-program-map.json. Those two read a library's SONAME and a program's
installed name, which only work while the component is still its own file.
This one reads the symbols an ELF exports, which is what is left when a
component has been linked into someone else's binary.
Measured need: the Zyxel GS1900-8 notice declares ncurses, readline and
quagga, and all three are inside one 400 KB executable, bin/cli. No version
string for any of them survives — the only version-shaped string in the whole
binary is the symbol-versioning tag GCC_3.0 — so signature identification
cannot see them and neither can a version-string pass. But the binary exports
1259 dynamic symbols, because its plugin libraries resolve back into it, and
46 of them are ncurses internals, 145 readline internals, 18 vtysh entry
points. The evidence is right there in the dynamic symbol table.
This does not make static linking generally readable. A binary that exports
nothing tells us nothing: MikroTik's bin/sshfs has FUSE linked in and exports
no dynamic symbols at all, so FUSE stays unfound. What this reads is the case
where the symbols survived.
Rules for adding entries:
- Prefer a component's internal symbols to its public API. The public API is
what a compatible reimplementation also provides: libedit exports readline's
rl_* entry points, and tgetent/tputs/tparm belong to every termcap there
has ever been. The internals do not travel — libedit has no _rl_dispatch,
and only ncurses has _nc_*.
- Give several, and require several to match. One shared name is a
coincidence; `min` of them together is not. It also survives vendor
patching, which is not hypothetical: Zyxel's quagga has cmd_init and
vty_out but no vty_init, and carries invented commands beside them.
- Only list a symbol seen in a real image. Every symbol below was read out
of a binary in the vendor corpus, not recalled from a header file.
- No versions, no purl, no CPE. A symbol set says a component is present,
never which release it is. These judgements are emitted as presence-only
for the same reason the SONAME ones are.
- Do not add a component whose SONAME or program name already finds it. The
cheaper evidence is also the plainer one for a reader to check.
- Names shared with a fork are a naming risk, not a CVE risk, because a
presence-only component carries no identifier for an advisory to match.
Where a fork exists it is called out below.

why: _nc_* is ncurses' own internal namespace. tgetent, tgetstr, tputs and tparm
are the termcap/terminfo API and are shared with every other implementation,
so none of them appear here.
Seen in: Zyxel GS1900-8 bin/cli (46 _nc_ symbols).
GNU readline's internals. The public rl_* entry points and add_history are
deliberately left out: libedit provides those under a readline-compatible
façade, and matching on them would report GNU readline for a BSD library.
_rl_* has no such counterpart.
Seen in: Zyxel GS1900-8 bin/cli (145 _rl_ symbols).
vtysh is quagga's integrated shell and ships as part of it, so its entry
points prove quagga is in the image. The command-library names (cmd_init,
install_element, vty_out) are listed too because a vendor may build the
library into a product without vtysh's own main.
FRRouting forked from quagga and keeps the same symbol names, so an FRR
image would be reported as quagga. The corpus case is quagga — bin/cli
carries the string 'Integrated shell for Quagga routing software suite.'
and bugzilla.quagga.net — and a presence-only component carries no
identifier, so the cost of the confusion is a wrong name in the notice, not
a wrong advisory. Recheck the strings before trusting the name.
Seen in: Zyxel GS1900-8 bin/cli (18 vtysh_ symbols).
